etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French consulte. In sense “council”, it represents Latin cōnsultum, Italian consulto; and it may have been often taken as a direct formation from the verb.

definitions.definition: (now US, countable) A visit to consult somebody, such as a doctor; a consultation.
(obsolete) The act of consulting or deliberating; consultation.

quote.citation: 1646, Thomas Browne, “Of the Iewes”, in Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], London:  […]  T[homas] H[arper] for Edward Dod, […], →OCLC, 4th book, page 201:
quote.text: For firſt upon conſult of reaſon, there will bee found no eaſie aſſurance for to faſten a materiall or temperamentall propriety upon any nation;  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The result of consultation; determination; decision.

quote.citation: a. 1701 (date written), John Dryden, “The First Book of Homer’s Ilias”, in The Miscellaneous Works of John Dryden, […], volume IV, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson, […], published 1760, →OCLC, page 431:
quote.text: [T]he council broke; / And all their grave conſults diſſolv'd in ſmoke.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A council; a meeting for consultation.

quote.citation: 1730, Jonathan Swift, chapter 5, in Death and Daphne:

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French consulter, from Latin cōnsultō (“to deliberate, consult”), frequentative of cōnsulō (“to consult, deliberate, consider, reflect upon, ask advice”), from com- (“together”) + -sulō, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“to take, grab”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To seek the opinion or advice of another; to take counsel; to deliberate together; to confer; to advise.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: Let us consult upon to-morrow's business.

quote.citation: 1661 (written), published in 1681, Thomas Hobbes, A Dialogue between a Philosopher and a Student of the Common Laws of England
quote.text: All the laws of England have been made by the kings of England, consulting with the nobility and commons.

quote.citation: 1889 January 11 [1888 December 21], Kung Taotai, “North Honan Road.”, in M. F. A. Fraser, transl., North-China Herald and Supreme Court & Consular Gazette‎[1], volume XLII, number 1119, Shanghai, →OCLC, page 37, column 1:
quote.text: SIR,—I have the honour to refer to your letter requesting me to desire Mr. Y. Ching-chong to come and consult with the Municipal Council, as Mr. Wood, the Chairman of that Body had informed you at a personal interview that they fully concurred in the desirability of co-operation with Mr. Ching-chong in improvements in the Honan road draining and lighting.

quote.citation: 1887, A[rthur] Conan Doyle, “A Study in Scarlet”, in Beeton’s Christmas Annual, London, New York, N.Y., Melbourne, Vic.: Ward, Lock & Co., part I (Being a reprint from the reminiscences of John H. Watson, M.D., […]), chapter II (The Science of Deduction), page 13:
quote.text: Well, I have a trade of my own. I suppose I am the only one in the world. I’m a consulting detective, if you can understand what that is.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To work as a consultant or contractor rather than as a full-time employee of a firm.
(transitive) To ask advice of; to seek the opinion of (a person)

quote.citation: 1899, John Cotton Dana, chapter 1, in A Library Primer:
quote.text: If you have no library commission, consult a lawyer and get from him a careful statement of what can be done under present statutory regulations.

quote.citation: 1904, Guy Wetmore Carryl, chapter 3, in Far from the Maddening Girls:
quote.text: Which reminds me that I have never remembered from that hour to consult the dictionary upon a selvage.

quote.citation: 1837, William Whewell, History of the Inductive Sciences:
quote.text: Men forgot, or feared, to consult nature, to seek for new truths, to do what the great discoverers of other times had done; they were content to consult libraries.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To have reference to, in judging or acting; to have regard to; to consider; as, to consult one's wishes.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We are  […]  to consult the necessities of life, rather than matters of ornament and delight.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To deliberate upon; to take for.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: Many things were there consulted for the future, yet nothing was positively resolved.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To bring about by counsel or contrivance; to devise; to contrive.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Habakkuk 2:10:
quote.text: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people.
